description:
We are a small team of second-year software engineering students. We enjoy building practical web and software projects and learning new tools as we go. We work well together, communicate openly, and like turning ideas into simple, working prototypes.
We would be happy to meet teammates who are interested in UI/UX design, data analysis, or space and Earth science, but anyone who is curious and wants to learn is welcome.
summary: Soundscape Earth turns NASA's Earth Information Center sea surface temperature map into live sound. As you move across the map with a mouse, a finger or the keyboard, the colour under your cursor is read back into a real temperature anomaly and turned into sound in real time: warmer-than-normal water sounds heartwarming, colder water sounds melancholy, normal water sounds calm. A 25-step timeline lets you hear how the same place has changed from 2002 to today, and on land two extra layers let you hear human presence and wildlife diversity. It was designed for everyone, and it is fully usable without sight: blind visitors get spoken guidance, keyboard navigation and screen reader announcements from the very first screen. Our goal is to let people not only see but hear and feel how our planet is changing.
details:
What it does

Soundscape Earth is a web app that pairs NASA Earth Information Center imagery with sound generated in real time. Users explore NASA's Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly map (SVS #5176) by moving over it. Every point is read from the original NASA picture: the pixel colour is matched against NASA's own colour scale and converted back into a temperature anomaly in °C (average conversion error: 0.012 °C). Land, ice and ocean are recognised separately.

How the sound works

No audio files are used; all sound is synthesised in the browser with the Web Audio API. Each kind of place has its own theme, chosen by our team: warm water is "heartwarming", cold water "melancholy", normal water "calm", ice "solitude", land "grounded". The theme sets the character of the sound, while the strength of the sound always follows the real value, so +0.5 °C sounds slightly warm and +4 °C sounds strongly warm. Longitude controls left/right stereo position. On land, two optional layers add sound for human presence (more people = more chaotic) and wildlife diversity (more mammal species = more alive and peaceful). A "Why does it sound like this?" panel explains, for the current point, which value produced which sound.

Time

A 25-step timeline shows the same day (13 November) for every year from 2002 to 2025, plus the latest available satellite data. A small chart shows how the selected point has changed over these years.

Accessibility

The first screen asks whether the visitor wants blind assistance (keys F/J). The whole app can be used with the keyboard; positions, values and themes are announced to screen readers; a built-in spoken guide explains the controls; reduced-motion preferences are respected.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Web Audio API, Canvas API, Leaflet (EPSG:4326), NASA GIBS map tiles, Natural Earth labels. Hosted on GitHub Pages. NASA images are stored locally in the project with a SOURCES.json file listing the origin and credit of every file.
